title: The CVs in the chat window
scenario:
You manage a recruiting team. Your company has an approved AI tool: a business account set up by IT, under a contract with the vendor. A recruiter tells you she has been pasting full candidate CVs (names, phone numbers, home addresses, work history) into an AI app on her personal account, to compare candidates faster. She says: "It's fine, I read that the vendor doesn't train on our data."

You need to decide what to do now and what the team rule should be.

questions.prompt: What is the main problem with what the recruiter did?

options.text: Personal data went to a vendor through a personal account, outside the terms the company agreed to.
options.explanation: Right. Data terms differ by product and plan. Anthropic's docs, for example, point consumer plans to a separate consumer data policy. The company's agreement covers its business account, not her personal one.

options.text: AI models can't read CVs, so the comparison is useless.
options.explanation: Models handle documents like CVs well. The problem is where the data went, not whether the task works.

options.text: There is no problem, because no vendor ever stores prompts.
options.explanation: Vendors may store some data. OpenAI's docs, for example, say abuse monitoring logs are kept for up to 30 days by default.

options.text: The only problem is that it cost the company money.
options.explanation: Cost is not the issue here. The risk is personal data shared under terms the company never approved.

questions.prompt: The recruiter says "the vendor doesn't train on our data." What is wrong with this as a reason?

options.text: Nothing. If data is not used for training, it is never stored.
options.explanation: Not training on data is different from not storing it. Vendors' docs describe retention for abuse monitoring, legal reasons and flagged content.

options.text: Vendors always train on all data.
options.explanation: That is false for the business API. OpenAI and Anthropic both say API data is not used for training without your permission or opt-in.

options.text: The no-training terms she read apply to business API use, and "no training" doesn't mean "not stored".
options.explanation: Right. The no-training statements in OpenAI's and Anthropic's docs are about API and business use. And both vendors describe cases where data is kept for a time.

options.text: The vendor's no-training promise covers every product the vendor sells.
options.explanation: Terms differ by product and plan. Anthropic's docs, for example, send consumer plans to a separate consumer data policy. A promise made for the business API does not cover a personal app.

questions.prompt: What is the best rule for the team going forward?

options.text: Ban all AI use in recruiting.
options.explanation: Too broad. The company already has an approved tool for this. The fix is to use it, with less personal data.

options.text: Use only the approved business account, remove contact details that the task doesn't need, and check with legal or IT before using AI on sensitive personal data.
options.explanation: Right. Approved account, minimum data, and sign-off for sensitive data. Comparing skills doesn't need a phone number or home address.

options.text: Keep using personal accounts, but delete the chats after.
options.explanation: Deleting a chat in the app doesn't change the terms the data was sent under, and vendors may keep some data for a time.

options.text: Turn on zero data retention in each recruiter's personal app settings.
options.explanation: ZDR is set up by the company with the vendor, and needs the vendor's approval. Anthropic's docs list consumer plans as not covered by its ZDR.
